Every endodontist has seen this. Here's what the evidence says about why.
r3
In a 2010 study of seventy-nine endodontic emergency patients, overall localization was about seventy-three percent.
r4
With periradicular symptoms, it was eighty-nine percent. Without them, just thirty percent.
r5
The pulp is innervated by A delta and C fibers, but it lacks proprioceptors. Pulpal pain signals that something is wrong, not where.
r6
Once inflammation reaches the periodontal ligament, its mechanoreceptors can localize the tooth. That's why percussion and bite tests carry so much weight.
r7
Owatz and colleagues found mechanical allodynia in fifty-seven percent of patients with irreversible pulpitis.
r8
Then there's convergence. Recording in cats, Sessle's group showed single neurons in subnucleus caudalis responding to tooth pulp, skin, mucosa, and muscle.
r9
And referral spreads as intensity rises. Sharav and Falace both found referral patterns weren't diagnostic, with extensive overlap between the arches.
So reproduce the chief complaint. Test adjacent and opposing teeth with cold, percussion, and bite tests. If it's still unclear, use selective anesthesia, starting with the maxillary arch.
Trust the tests, not the finger.
